subject: Biotechnology
title: Gene Cloning Basics
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Gene Cloning Basics.

hook.text: Gene cloning does not mean cloning animals — it means making identical copies of a single gene.

buildup.text: A gene is inserted into a plasmid — a small circular DNA that bacteria replicate alongside their own.

discovery.text: As bacteria divide, every daughter cell carries the plasmid — amplifying the gene millions of times.

twist.text: Antibiotic resistance genes on the plasmid act as selectors — only bacteria carrying it survive the drug.

climax.text: Gene cloning enabled the biotech industry — every recombinant drug starts with a cloned gene in a plasmid.

punchline.text: Clone the gene, grow the bacteria, harvest the product.

quiz.question: What is a plasmid in gene cloning?
options: A type of virus used to deliver genes to humans
A small circular DNA molecule that bacteria replicate, carrying the inserted gene
A chemical used to dissolve cell membranes

details.summary: Gene cloning inserts a gene of interest into a circular DNA molecule called a plasmid, which is then introduced into bacteria that replicate it with every cell division. This produces millions of identical copies of the gene for study, modification, or protein production.
details.whyItMatters: Gene cloning is the foundational technique that launched the recombinant DNA revolution. It enables the production of human insulin in bacteria, the study of individual genes, and the creation of genetically modified organisms.
takeaways: Target genes are inserted into plasmid vectors using restriction enzymes and ligase
Bacteria replicate plasmids, producing millions of gene copies overnight
Cloned genes can be expressed to produce recombinant proteins

faq.question: What are restriction enzymes and why are they essential for cloning?
faq.answer: Restriction enzymes are molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. They allow scientists to precisely cut both the target gene and the plasmid vector at matching sites, enabling the gene to be inserted into the vector using DNA ligase.

faq.question: How do scientists know which bacteria successfully took up the plasmid?
faq.answer: Plasmids carry antibiotic resistance genes as selectable markers. Bacteria are grown on plates containing that antibiotic. Only cells that successfully took up the plasmid survive, allowing easy identification and selection of clones containing the desired gene.
